overview: Medieval Prussians were Western Baltic communities, distinct from the later German kingdom. Regional groups had different histories. Trading settlements, burials and later writings illuminate particular places and periods.

periods.title: Earlier trade and connected settlements
periods.summary: Truso developed before this atlas interval; the narrative also follows its activity into the early eleventh century.

periods.title: Regional communities
periods.summary: Baltic-speaking groups occupied several lands rather than one centralized Prussian kingdom.

periods.title: Later conquest
periods.summary: The Teutonic Order’s thirteenth-century conquest followed this map segment; communities survived under new rulers.

sections.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds

items.text: At Truso, near modern Elbląg, excavators found rows of timber houses and working areas. Most evidence dates before or around 1000. The port connected Scandinavian and Baltic networks; it should not stand for every Prussian village.

Some Truso houses had three rooms, with hearths and loom remains indicating different activities. Households needed space for work and storage as well as sleep. The archaeological plans reveal arrangements that written accounts rarely describe.

The port preserved remains of clinker-built boats, whose overlapping planks were joined with iron rivets. Surviving details suggest vessels around nine to eleven metres long. Boatbuilding knowledge supported the movement of goods and people.

Truso’s combs and weights can be compared with finds from other Baltic ports. Matching types help investigate connections and chronology, but a familiar object design does not identify an individual owner’s birthplace or language.

The settlement’s drainage ditch removed excess water and divided areas of activity. The nearby stream was also regulated. Keeping a working waterfront usable required routine control of water, as well as boats and successful trading.

Truso smiths used imported iron bars and local bog iron to make tools and weapons. Weaving traces occur in many buildings. Manufacturing belonged inside the settlement’s daily work; trade was not simply waiting for a foreign ship to unload.

An illustrated mid-eleventh-century grave assemblage from Irzekapinis in Sambia includes weapons, horse equipment, pottery and parts of weighing equipment. Their association records one burial’s treatment. It does not tell us what every person owned during life.
Regional groups included Sambians, Natangians and Bartians. Local leadership and assemblies varied; one atlas colour simplifies communities that did not share a centralized national government.

Missionaries Adalbert and Bruno died in 997 and 1009 during missions in the region or its borderlands. Christian accounts preserve these events through the particular viewpoints of missionary writers.

sections.title: A language survives in later pages

items.text: Kayle rekyse is an Old Prussian greeting, translated “Hello, mister!” in the study of the Basel Epigram. It appears on folio 63ra of manuscript F.V.2 beside a text dated 1369. This attested sample is later than the atlas’s 1000 to 1200 interval.

The epigram’s handwriting and several readings are debated. Comparing letter shapes and paper watermarks helps scholars test interpretations. Its playful greeting belongs to a particular manuscript setting, not a reconstructed conversation invented for medieval Prussians.

Longer Old Prussian texts survive in sixteenth-century Christian catechisms; the Elbing vocabulary records words with German equivalents. These later documents preserve language knowledge while also reflecting the religious and educational purposes of their compilers.

ending.text: The Teutonic Order conquered the Prussian lands during the thirteenth century, after the atlas segment ends. War, displacement and unequal rule transformed communities, but people and their language survived for generations. Later language loss and assimilation were processes, not a disappearance of everyone in one conquest year.
